newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK RPI data for April.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK RPI data for April.

text.p: Following is a list of analysts' reactions to UK retail price inflation data for April released at 0830 GMT.
* UK APR RPI +0.6% MM,+2.4% YY, RPIX +0.6% MM,+2.5% YY, RPIY +0.3% MM,+2.0% YY (vs expectations RPI +0.6 +2.5, RPIX YY 2.6, RPIY YY 2.2)

GLENN DAVIES, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT CREDIT LYONNAIS - "The figures are defintely somewhat better than expected... We were saying that April was something of a volatile month so there was scope there for a bit of a surprise."

"I don't think there are any worries about inflation in the traded goods sector. Import prices are obviously getting squeezed by the strength of the pound and manufactured goods in general squeezed by the fact that the rise in sterling means that UK industry is starting to lose competitiveness.
But if you look at services that is the part of the economy that is growing very strongly at the moment.... and that's where I think the inflation worry really is," Davies added.

PHILIP SHAW, ECONOMIST AT UNION PLC - "The report shows a continued decline in the underlying rate of inflation with the 2.5 per cent target being hit. The short term outlook for inflation remains stable with the strength of sterling keeping a lid on prices. Nevertheless, policy still needs to be tightened for the inflation target to be achieved in the long term."

JEREMY HAWKINS, BANK OF AMERICA - "The RPI data were a touch softer than expected and may be a small positive for the UK interest rate markets. Impact on the pound is likely to be negligible..... The decline in the headline rate was led by the fall in motoring as petrol prices fell, and leisure goods.

Seasonal food was a touch above the level seen last year. The high street showed a relatively healthy picture, with the fall in household goods greater than than seen in 1996 and clothing and footwear matching the rise in prices seen last year. Inflation in these sectors is 1.4 per cent and 1.1 per cent respectively. This suggests that the strength in consumer spending and the buoyancy of the housing market is having limited impact on prices.

The service sector continues to show the greatest increase, with overall inflation here at 3.3 per cent versus the 1.7 per cent evident for the goods sector. These data suggest no immediate urgency to raise interest rates, though the Bank of England is clearly concerned that the pace of growth will lead to future inflation."
